facebook.long_form:
FERRARI REVEALS MICHAEL SCHUMACHER TRIBUTE FOR MONZA — AND IT'S STUNNING

One week before the Italian Grand Prix, Ferrari has pulled back the curtain on what might be the most emotionally powerful livery in recent Formula 1 memory.

The SF-26 will run in a special Michael Schumacher tribute design at Monza, inspired by the iconic F310 — the car Schumacher drove in his first season with Ferrari back in 1996. The color scheme features red and black detailing with gold wheels, a dramatic departure from the team's standard 2026 appearance.

The tribute doesn't stop at the car. Race suits worn by Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will feature seven stars on the back — one for each of Schumacher's world championship titles — along with his personal logo on the waist beneath the race numbers of both drivers.

This year carries double significance: 2026 marks 30 years since Schumacher first drove for the Scuderia, and 20 years since his final season in red. He won 72 of his 91 career victories at Ferrari, claimed five consecutive world titles between 2000 and 2004, and memorably announced his retirement at Monza in 2006 following his penultimate win for the team.

Ferrari also has a strategic dimension to this weekend: the team is expected to debut its ADUO-2 power unit, delivering approximately 15 additional horsepower and an estimated 0.2 seconds per lap — the biggest upgrade of the 2026 season. At Monza, the most power-sensitive circuit on the calendar, that could matter enormously.

Emotionally charged. Strategically loaded. This is going to be a week to remember.

facebook.long_form:
HAMILTON APOLOGIZES AFTER DUTCH GP RADIO FURY — FERRARI NEEDS A RESET

Lewis Hamilton knows he crossed a line at Zandvoort, and he's said so publicly.

After finishing P4 at the Dutch Grand Prix — just off the podium in a race where the top three was Lando Norris, Kimi Antonelli, and George Russell — Hamilton was furious with Ferrari's strategy. The root of the frustration: Charles Leclerc and Hamilton were on different tyre strategies, and Leclerc refused a team order to let his teammate through. Hamilton lost critical time behind Leclerc on track, costing him a realistic shot at third place.

The radio messages that followed were damning. "Great way of wasting time guys, good job," Hamilton said sarcastically on team radio. He went further in the media afterward, criticizing Ferrari's driver management and invoking his former team Mercedes as a comparison point.

In his apology, Hamilton was direct: "In the heat of the moment frustration can come out, especially when you care as deeply as I do. But that wasn't the best version of me. I take responsibility for that, and I'll be better."

It's the right message. But it raises real questions heading into Monza — Ferrari's home race, a weekend loaded with the Schumacher tribute and the ADUO-2 power unit debut. The team needs Hamilton and Leclerc pulling in the same direction. A P4 at Zandvoort with more friction than results is not the momentum Ferrari wanted.

Monza is six days away. The reset starts now.

[Window: 12:00 PM ET]

facebook.long_form:
ANTONELLI LEADS BY 59 — AND MERCEDES WON'T PLAY FAVORITES

Kimi Antonelli is sitting on 242 points at the top of the 2026 Drivers' Championship, 59 clear of teammate George Russell. And Mercedes has made one thing very clear: that lead does not entitle Antonelli to preferential treatment.

The team has confirmed it will not impose team orders to favor Antonelli's title bid. In a season where the young Italian has already made history — becoming the youngest driver ever to lead the F1 World Championship — the decision to keep the fight fair within the team is both a sporting statement and a strategic gamble.

Here's why it matters at Monza: Antonelli carries a grid penalty for exceeding his power unit allocation. He will start from the back of the grid at a race where catching up is possible but points against his main rivals are not guaranteed. Russell starts from wherever his pace puts him. Hamilton — 59 points behind Antonelli — is in the same position.

With 11 races remaining, the math still heavily favors Antonelli. But Monza, with the grid penalty and a circuit where strategy and pace can produce unusual results, is the kind of race where a 59-point lead can become 30 in an afternoon — or 80 if Antonelli charges through the field.

The internal Mercedes battle is one of the most compelling subplots of the 2026 season. And it will be fully on display in Italy next weekend.

facebook.long_form:
MONZA IS ONE WEEK AWAY — HERE'S WHAT MAKES THIS ITALIAN GP SO ELECTRIC

September 4-6, Circuit de Monza, Italy. The Temple of Speed. Ferrari's home race. And this year, the Italian Grand Prix arrives with more storylines than any single weekend can comfortably contain.

Start with the on-track dynamics. Antonelli — championship leader by 59 points — faces the worst grid slot possible at the circuit most rewarding for recovery drives. Monza's long straights and minimal corner count make overtaking viable in ways most circuits don't allow, so a last-place start doesn't necessarily mean a catastrophic result. But points lost to Russell and Hamilton at Ferrari's home race would be a significant psychological and mathematical blow.

Then there's Ferrari. The Scuderia arrives carrying a special Schumacher tribute livery and, more critically, the ADUO-2 power unit — the largest single upgrade of the season. At Monza, where straight-line speed is everything and the power unit matters more than almost anywhere else on the calendar, that 15-horsepower gain could translate directly into race positions for Hamilton and Leclerc.

Mercedes, meanwhile, is still processing what happened at Zandvoort, where the team was left "head-scratching" by unexpected performance weaknesses. At a circuit so different from the Netherlands, it's unclear whether those issues carry over.

Eleven races to go. The second half of the 2026 season is where championships are won and lost. Monza is the opening statement.

[Window: 5:00 PM ET]

facebook.long_form:
THE MONACO APPEAL VERDICT IS STILL COMING — AND IT COULD CHANGE EVERYTHING

More than two months after the Monaco Grand Prix, the controversy over Pierre Gasly's third-place finish still has no final resolution.

The International Court of Appeal heard arguments from McLaren and Red Bull on August 25 in Paris, but no verdict was issued. A decision is expected in approximately two to three weeks from the hearing date — placing the likely ruling around mid-September, as F1 heads into the run of back-to-back grands prix following Monza.

The core of the dispute: FOM (Formula One Management) admitted to a pitlane distance measurement error that formed the basis of Gasly's original penalty during the Monaco race. Gasly — driving for Alpine — was penalized and then reclassified, ultimately holding onto P3. McLaren and Red Bull believe the ruling was incorrect and that the error-based penalty shouldn't stand.

If the appeal succeeds, Monaco race results could be adjusted, which means championship points shift retroactively. In a season where 59 points separates the leader from second place, any redistribution matters.

Gasly holds P3 for now. The ICA holds the pen. And the verdict could land right in the middle of F1's most critical stretch of the season.

[Window: 8:00 PM ET]
